newsitem.title: UK: Kurds warned US they would turn to Iraq -- daily.
newsitem.headline: Kurds warned US they would turn to Iraq -- daily.

text.p: Senior United States officials were warned by Kurdish leaders that they could turn to Iraq for aid if Washington did not support them against rivals backed by Iran, Britain's Independent newspaper reported on Friday.

It said letters sent by the Kurdish Democratic Party (KDP) to U.S. policymakers in the week before Iraqi forces backed the KDP in its capture of Arbil, Iraqi Kurdistan's largest city, contained warnings the group could go to Baghdad for support.
The newspaper said the correspondence, of which it printed extracts, could stir up controversy over reports Washington was taken by surprise by the intervention of the Iraqi army in the conflict.
The Iraqi intervention prompted U.S. cruise missile attacks on targets south of Baghdad on Tuesday and Wednesday.
Rival Kurdish factions continued to skirmish in northern Iraq on Friday as the United States appeared to back away from further air strikes to punish Iraq for its offensive.
But aid workers said the polarisation of the two main factions, with one turning to Baghdad and the other to Tehran, could signal a loosening of the West's hold over the region.
The KDP's rivals, the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) of Kurdish militia leader Jalal Talabani, have warned they are prepared to seek Iranian help if necessary to fight back.

But the Independent said the KDP of Kurdish chieftain Massoud Barzani warned the United States before its missile attacks that Iran was already supporting the PUK, and that his faction would turn to Baghdad for support if Washington did nothing.
The paper said the KDP sent a memo to U.S. officials before the attack on Arbil saying: "Our options are limited...
"Since the U.S. is not responding even politically... the only option left is the Iraqis."

The newspaper said that U.S. officials appeared to remain relaxed as the situation deteriorated in northern Iraq over several months despite a series of communications between the KDP and the U.S. administration.

U.S. officials who received the correspondence included Robert Deutsch, director of the Office of Northern Gulf Affairs, and Robert Pelletreau, Assistant Secretary of State for Near East Affairs, the paper said.

In the end, despite last-minute talks at the U.S. embassy in London on August 30, the KDP turned to its former enemy, Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein, for help. A day after the talks, KDP fighters backed by Iraqi tanks moved into Arbil.
U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said the United States reserved the right to strike at Iraq again if Baghdad tried to re-build the air defences disabled by the U.S. missile raids.
In Washington, U.S. intelligence chief John Deutch told the Senate Intelligence Committee that Iraqi troops were now pulling out of northern Iraq, a view disputed by the PUK.
